entities.name: United Russia
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
United Russia (Yedinaya Rossiya), founded 2001 by the merger of three pro-Kremlin parties under Vladimir Putin's patronage, is Russia's dominant governing party — holding 324 of 450 State Duma seats (2021), providing the institutional architecture for Putin's political system, and functioning less as an ideological party than as a 'party of power' that aggregates bureaucratic, military, and business elites around the presidential office. United Russia is the world's largest right-wing governing party by membership (2 million members) and the institutional backbone of Putin's system.

United Russia was created in 2001 through the merger of Unity (Yedinstvo, founded 1999 immediately before the 1999 Duma elections to support Putin) with Fatherland-All Russia (Otechestvo-Vsya Rossiya). Its 2003 Duma supermajority was achieved through a combination of genuine popularity (Putin's approval ratings 70-80%) and systematic voter manipulation. The party's ideology — 'conservatism' and 'sovereign democracy' — was formulated by Kremlin political technologist Vladislav Surkov.

United Russia's paradox: Putin himself is not formally a member (though he chairs the party and endorses its candidates), creating the unusual fiction of a party-of-power whose leader stands above the party. The party's 2011 protest crisis — when massive protests followed fraudulent Duma elections (the 'For Fair Elections' protests, December 2011-January 2012) — briefly threatened its dominance. Opposition blogger Alexei Navalny called it the 'Party of Crooks and Thieves,' a label that spread widely. The 2022 Ukraine invasion was unanimously supported by United Russia Duma members.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: United Russia — the world's largest right-wing governing party, designed by Kremlin political technologists as a party-of-power apparatus rather than an ideological movement — is the definitive institutional model for 21st-century authoritarian 'managed democracy,' where electoral competition exists within a system designed to guarantee one outcome.
